Split the powers so that **tan x** and **sec²x** appear — then one substitution finishes
it.
**Step 1 — rewrite the integrand.**
sinⁿx/cos^(n+2)x = (sinⁿx/cosⁿx) × (1/cos²x)
= **tanⁿx · sec²x**
**Step 2 — substitute.** Let **u = tan x**, so **du = sec²x dx**:
∫ tanⁿx sec²x dx = ∫ uⁿ du
**Step 3 — integrate by the power rule.**
= u^(n+1)/(n + 1) + C
**Step 4 — substitute back.**
= **tan^(n+1)x/(n + 1) + C** ✓
**Check by differentiating.**
d/dx[tan^(n+1)x/(n + 1)] = (n + 1)tanⁿx · sec²x/(n + 1)
= tanⁿx sec²x
= (sinⁿx/cosⁿx)(1/cos²x)
= **sinⁿx/cos^(n+2)x** ✓ the integrand exactly.
**Why the exponent must be n + 1.** Integrating uⁿ **raises** the power by one, so the
answer carries tan^(n+1)x — and the denominator must be the **new** exponent, n + 1. That
pairing is the signature of the power rule, and three of the four options break it:
**tan^(n−1)x/(n − 1)** ✗ — the power has gone **down**, which is differentiation, not
integration.
**tanⁿx/n** ✗ — the power is unchanged.
**tan^(n+2)x/(n + 2)** ✗ — consistent in itself, but it would be the integral of
tan^(n+1)x sec²x, one power too high.
**Why the n + 2 in the original denominator matters.** It is exactly what supplies the
**sec²x**: splitting cos^(n+2) into cosⁿ × cos² leaves one factor of 1/cos²x = sec²x,
which is precisely du. Had the denominator been cos^(n+1)x, the leftover would be
1/cos x = sec x and the substitution would not close.
**A check with n = 1.** Then the integral is ∫sin x/cos³x dx, which by the formula is
tan²x/2 + C. Differentiating: tan x sec²x = (sin x/cos x)(1/cos²x) = sin x/cos³x ✓
∴ tan^(n+1)x/(n + 1) + C.

kcet|Mathematics|2004|1||0|0:
When three expressions are equal, give the common value a name — the condition then
unlocks in one line.
**Step 1 — name the common ratio.** Let
log x/(a − b) = log y/(b − c) = log z/(c − a) = **k**
**Step 2 — read off each logarithm.**
log x = **k(a − b)**
log y = **k(b − c)**
log z = **k(c − a)**
**Step 3 — add them.** The logarithm of a product is the sum of the logarithms:
log(xyz) = log x + log y + log z
= k[(a − b) + (b − c) + (c − a)]
**Step 4 — notice the bracket collapses.** Every letter appears once positively and once
negatively:
(a − b) + (b − c) + (c − a) = a − b + b − c + c − a = **0**
so
log(xyz) = k × 0 = **0**
**Step 5 — exponentiate.**
xyz = e⁰ = **1** ✓
**Why the bracket had to vanish.** The three denominators a − b, b − c and c − a are a
**cyclic** set, and such a set always sums to zero — each letter is added once and
subtracted once as the cycle closes. That is the whole design of the question.
**A worked instance.** Take a = 3, b = 1, c = 2 and k = 1. Then
log x = 3 − 1 = **2**, so x = e²
log y = 1 − 2 = **−1**, so y = e⁻¹
log z = 2 − 3 = **−1**, so z = e⁻¹
xyz = e² × e⁻¹ × e⁻¹ = e⁰ = **1** ✓
**Why the answer is 1 and not 0.** The **logarithm** is zero, and the number whose
logarithm is zero is **1**, not 0. Option (1), 0, is the value of log(xyz) — the answer
one step short of the question, and the likeliest slip. Note also that xyz could never be
0, since each of x, y, z is an exponential and so strictly positive.
**A related identity.** The same method shows that x^(b−c) y^(c−a) z^(a−b) = 1 as well,
and more generally that any cyclically weighted product of this family reduces to 1.
∴ 1.

"Equal intercepts on the axes" fixes the form of the line before the point is used at
all.
**Step 1 — write the intercept form.** A line with x-intercept a and y-intercept b is
x/a + y/b = 1
Setting the two intercepts **equal**, b = a:
x/a + y/a = 1
Multiplying by a:
**x + y = a**
So every such line has the form x + y = constant, with **gradient −1**.
**Step 2 — use the point (2, 4).**
2 + 4 = a
**a = 6**
**Step 3 — write the line.**
x + y = 6, that is **x + y − 6 = 0** ✓
**Check.** The intercepts are x = 6 (setting y = 0) and y = 6 (setting x = 0) — **equal**
✓ and the point (2, 4) satisfies 2 + 4 = 6 ✓
**Reading the options by their gradients.** Every line with equal intercepts has gradient
**−1**, so the coefficients of x and y must be the **same**:
**4x − y − 4 = 0** ✗ gradient 4
**2x + y − 8 = 0** ✗ gradient −2
**x + y − 6 = 0** ✓ gradient −1
**x + 2y − 10 = 0** ✗ gradient −1/2
That single test identifies the answer without using the point at all — and the point then
confirms the constant.
**The degenerate case worth noting.** A line through the **origin**, such as y = −x, also
has "equal intercepts", both zero. The question's point (2, 4) is not on y = −x, so that
case does not arise here; but in some versions of this problem both families must be
considered.
**Why the intercept form is the right starting point.** Writing the line as y = mx + c and
imposing equal intercepts means solving c = −c/m, giving m = −1 — the same conclusion, but
with a division that needs m ≠ 0. The intercept form reaches it directly.
∴ x + y − 6 = 0.

Use the standard formula for the area of a triangle from its three vertices, then solve
the resulting modulus equation.
**Step 1 — state the formula.**
area = ½|x₁(y₂ − y₃) + x₂(y₃ − y₁) + x₃(y₁ − y₂)|
**Step 2 — substitute** (x, 0), (1, 1) and (0, 2):
area = ½|x(1 − 2) + 1(2 − 0) + 0(0 − 1)|
= ½|−x + 2 + 0|
= **½|2 − x|**
**Step 3 — set it equal to 4.**
½|2 − x| = 4
**|2 − x| = 8**
**Step 4 — solve the modulus equation**, which splits into two cases:
2 − x = 8 ⟹ **x = −6**
2 − x = −8 ⟹ **x = 10**
**Step 5 — match against the options.** Only **−6** is offered ✓
**Check with x = −6.** The vertices are (−6, 0), (1, 1), (0, 2):
area = ½|(−6)(1 − 2) + 1(2 − 0) + 0(0 − 1)|
= ½|6 + 2 + 0|
= ½(8) = **4** ✓
**Check that x = 10 also works**, confirming the algebra:
area = ½|10(−1) + 2 + 0| = ½|−8| = **4** ✓ Both values are genuine; the question says
"a value of x", acknowledging that there are two.
**Why there are two answers.** The point (x, 0) slides along the **x-axis**, and the line
through (1, 1) and (0, 2) is fixed. The area grows in proportion to the distance from
(x, 0) to that line, and a given distance is reached on **either side** of the line's
x-intercept. Solving |2 − x| = 8 captures both.
**Testing the other options quickly.**
x = −2: area = ½|2 + 2| = **2** ✗
x = −4: area = ½|2 + 4| = **3** ✗
x = 8: area = ½|2 − 8| = **3** ✗
The area varies **linearly** with x away from x = 2, increasing by 1/2 for each unit, so
reaching 4 requires moving **8** units from x = 2 ✓ giving −6 or 10 directly.
∴ −6.

This is the standard limit **lim(1 + a/t)^t = e^a** in disguise — the task is to get the
expression into that shape.
**Step 1 — substitute to simplify the denominator.** Let **t = x − 1**, so x = t + 1 and
t → ∞ as x → ∞. The exponent becomes
3x − 1 = 3(t + 1) − 1 = **3t + 2**
and the limit is
lim(t→∞) [1 − 4/t]^(3t + 2)
**Step 2 — split the exponent.**
[1 − 4/t]^(3t + 2) = ([1 − 4/t]^t)³ × [1 − 4/t]²
**Step 3 — take the limit of each factor.**
[1 − 4/t]^t → **e^(−4)** (the standard limit with a = −4)
[1 − 4/t]² → (1 − 0)² = **1**
**Step 4 — combine.**
limit = (e^(−4))³ × 1 = **e^(−12)** ✓
**Why the exponent 3x − 1 contributes only its leading term.** The "−1" becomes "+2" after
the substitution, and [1 − 4/t]² tends to 1 because the base itself tends to 1 and the
exponent is **fixed**. Only the part of the exponent that grows **in proportion to t**
survives into the answer — here the 3t, giving the factor 3 in e^(−12).
**The quick rule.** For lim(x→∞) [1 + a/x]^(bx) the answer is **e^(ab)**, and the same
holds when x is shifted by a constant or the exponent carries a constant term. Here
a = **−4** and b = **3**, so ab = **−12** ✓ in one step.
**Checking the sign.** The base 1 − 4/(x − 1) is **less than 1** for large x, so raising
it to a large positive power drives it **towards zero** — the limit must therefore be
**less than 1**, which means a **negative** exponent on e ✓ That observation alone rules
out options (1), (3) and (4), all of which exceed 1.
**A numerical check at x = 1001.** Then 1 − 4/1000 = 0·996 and the exponent is 3002, so
0·996^3002 = e^(3002 × ln 0·996) = e^(3002 × (−0·004008)) = e^(−12·03) ✓ converging to
e^(−12) ≈ **6·14 × 10⁻⁶**.
∴ e^(−12).

A **diameter** of a circle passes through its centre, so two diameters meet **at** the
centre.
**Step 1 — find the centre** by solving the two diameter equations simultaneously.
x + y = 6 … (i)
x + 2y = 4 … (ii)
Subtracting (i) from (ii):
y = **−2**
and then from (i): x = 6 − (−2) = **8**
**centre = (8, −2)**
**Step 2 — find the radius** as the distance from the centre to the given point (6, 2):
r = √[(8 − 6)² + (−2 − 2)²]
= √[2² + (−4)²]
= √(4 + 16)
= **√20** ✓
(which is 2√5 ≈ 4·47.)
**Check.** The circle is (x − 8)² + (y + 2)² = 20. Testing (6, 2):
(6 − 8)² + (2 + 2)² = 4 + 16 = **20** ✓ the point lies on it.
Testing the centre against both diameters: 8 + (−2) = **6** ✓ and 8 + 2(−2) = **4** ✓
**Why the two lines must meet at the centre.** Every diameter is a chord through the
centre, so the centre lies on each of them — and two distinct non-parallel lines meet at
exactly one point ✓ (These two are not parallel: their gradients are −1 and −1/2.)
**Reading the distractors.** **20** is r², not r — the answer with the square root
forgotten, and the commonest error here. **4** and **6** are neither: 4 would need the
point at distance 4, and 6 is the constant from the first diameter's equation.
A quick check of size: the distance from (8, −2) to (6, 2) is the hypotenuse of a
2-by-4 right triangle, so it lies between 4 and 6 ✓ and √20 ≈ 4·47 does, while 20 plainly
does not.
∴ √20.

The two exponents **sin²x and cos²x add to 1**, so the two powers of 81 are reciprocals
up to a factor — which turns the equation into a quadratic.
**Step 1 — exploit the identity.** Since cos²x = 1 − sin²x,
81^(cos²x) = 81^(1 − sin²x) = 81/81^(sin²x)
**Step 2 — substitute.** Let **t = 81^(sin²x)**, so the equation becomes
t + 81/t = 30
**Step 3 — clear the fraction.**
t² − 30t + 81 = 0
**Step 4 — solve.** The discriminant is 900 − 324 = **576 = 24²**:
t = (30 ± 24)/2
**t = 27** or **t = 3**
**Step 5 — convert back.** Writing 81 = 3⁴, so 81^(sin²x) = 3^(4sin²x):
**t = 27 = 3³:** 4sin²x = 3 ⟹ sin²x = 3/4 ⟹ sin x = ±√3/2
**t = 3 = 3¹:** 4sin²x = 1 ⟹ sin²x = 1/4 ⟹ sin x = ±1/2
**Step 6 — apply the range 0 ≤ x ≤ π**, where sin x ≥ 0:
sin x = √3/2 ⟹ x = **π/3** or **2π/3**
sin x = 1/2 ⟹ x = **π/6** or **5π/6**
**Step 7 — match the options.** Of these four, only **π/6** is offered ✓
**Check x = π/6.** sin²(π/6) = 1/4 and cos²(π/6) = 3/4, so
81^(1/4) + 81^(3/4) = 3 + 27 = **30** ✓
**Testing the other options.**
**π/2:** sin² = 1, cos² = 0, giving 81 + 1 = **82** ✗
**π/4:** both are 1/2, giving 9 + 9 = **18** ✗
**3π/4:** same as π/4 by symmetry, **18** ✗
**Why 18 is the minimum.** By AM–GM, t + 81/t ≥ 2√81 = **18**, with equality when t = 9,
that is sin²x = 1/2. So the sum can never fall below 18 — and the equation = 30 therefore
has solutions on **either side** of x = π/4, which is exactly the four values found ✓
∴ π/6.

The square root in the exponent calls for the substitution **t = √x**, which turns the
integral into a polynomial-times-exponential handled by parts.
**Step 1 — substitute.** Let **t = √x**, so x = t² and **dx = 2t dt**:
∫ √x e^√x dx = ∫ t · e^t · 2t dt = **2∫ t² e^t dt**
**Step 2 — integrate by parts twice.** The standard result is
∫ t² e^t dt = e^t(t² − 2t + 2)
(obtained by taking u = t², dv = e^t dt, then repeating on the remaining ∫2t e^t dt.)
**Step 3 — multiply by 2.**
= 2e^t(t² − 2t + 2)
**Step 4 — substitute back**, with t = √x and t² = x:
= 2e^√x(x − 2√x + 2)
= **(2x − 4√x + 4) e^√x + c** ✓
**Check by differentiating.** With y = (2x − 4√x + 4)e^√x:
dy/dx = (2 − 2/√x)e^√x + (2x − 4√x + 4)e^√x × 1/(2√x)
= e^√x[2 − 2/√x + x/√x − 2 + 2/√x]
= e^√x[√x]
= **√x e^√x** ✓ the integrand exactly, with all the other terms cancelling in pairs.
**The by-parts pattern, worth knowing.** For any polynomial p(t),
∫p(t)e^t dt = e^t[p(t) − p′(t) + p″(t) − ⋯]
the signs alternating until the derivatives run out. With p = t²:
e^t[t² − 2t + 2] ✓ in one line, with no repeated integration at all.
**Why the answer has three terms.** Each differentiation of t² produces a new term, and t²
takes **two** differentiations to vanish — hence the three terms x, −2√x and 2, doubled to
2x, −4√x and 4.
**Reading the distractors.** Option (1) is not even of the right shape: it has a bare
2√x outside the exponential. Option (3) has **+4√x**, missing the alternating minus from
the by-parts pattern. Option (4), (1 − 4√x)e^√x, has only two terms where three are
needed. Differentiating each candidate is the quickest check, and only one returns
√x e^√x.
∴ (2x − 4√x + 4)e^√x + c.

The terms 9, −3, 1, −1/3, … form a **geometric progression** with a negative ratio, so
the infinite sum converges.
**Step 1 — identify a and r.**
first term **a = 9**
ratio r = −3/9 = **−1/3** (and checking the next: 1/(−3) = −1/3 ✓, and (−1/3)/1 = −1/3 ✓)
**Step 2 — check convergence.** |r| = 1/3 < 1 ✓ so the sum to infinity exists.
**Step 3 — apply the formula.**
S∞ = a/(1 − r)
= 9/(1 − (−1/3))
= 9/(1 + 1/3)
= 9/(4/3)
= 9 × 3/4
= **27/4** ✓
(which is 6·75.)
**Check by adding the first few terms.**
9
9 − 3 = **6**
6 + 1 = **7**
7 − 1/3 = **6·667**
6·667 + 1/9 = **6·778**
6·778 − 1/27 = **6·741**
The partial sums oscillate about **6·75** and close in on it ✓ — the alternation is
characteristic of a negative ratio, with the sum approached from both sides.
**The commonest error.** Taking r = +1/3, which gives S∞ = 9/(1 − 1/3) = 9/(2/3) =
**27/2 = 13·5** — far too large, since the series' terms alternate and partly cancel. The
sign of r is the whole question, and the alternating signs in 9, −3, 1, −1/3 make it
negative ✓
**A size check that settles it.** The first two terms alone give 9 − 3 = **6**, and all
the remaining terms together are smaller than 1 + 1/3 + 1/9 + ⋯ = 1·5 in magnitude. So the
sum must lie between about 6 and 7·5 ✓ Of the options, **9** is too big, **9/2 = 4·5** too
small, **15/2 = 7·5** at the very edge, and **27/4 = 6·75** sits comfortably inside.
∴ 27/4.

kcet|Mathematics|2005|6||0|0:
Powers of 2 repeat their remainders on division by 5 in a short **cycle**, so reduce the
exponent modulo the cycle length.
**Step 1 — compute the first few remainders.**
2¹ = 2 → remainder **2**
2² = 4 → remainder **4**
2³ = 8 = 5 + 3 → remainder **3**
2⁴ = 16 = 15 + 1 → remainder **1**
2⁵ = 32 = 30 + 2 → remainder **2** — the pattern repeats
So the cycle is **2, 4, 3, 1** with length **4**.
**Step 2 — reduce the exponent modulo 4.**
301 = 4 × 75 + **1**
so 2³⁰¹ has the same remainder as **2¹**.
**Step 3 — read it off.**
remainder = **2** ✓
**A cleaner argument.** Since 2⁴ = 16 ≡ 1 (mod 5),
2³⁰¹ = 2^(4×75 + 1) = (2⁴)⁷⁵ × 2 ≡ 1⁷⁵ × 2 = **2** (mod 5) ✓
**A third route, through the binomial theorem.**
2³⁰¹ = 2 × 2³⁰⁰ = 2 × (2⁴)⁷⁵ = 2 × 16⁷⁵ = 2 × (15 + 1)⁷⁵
Expanding (15 + 1)⁷⁵, every term except the last contains a factor of 15 and so is
divisible by 5; the last term is 1. Hence 16⁷⁵ leaves remainder **1**, and 2³⁰¹ leaves
remainder 2 × 1 = **2** ✓
**Why the cycle has length 4.** The remainders of 2ⁿ modulo 5 must repeat, and they cannot
repeat sooner than the first return to 1, which happens at n = 4. This is Fermat's little
theorem in miniature: for a prime p and a not divisible by p, a^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p), and
here p = 5 gives 2⁴ ≡ 1 ✓
**Reading the distractors.** A remainder on division by 5 must be **0, 1, 2, 3 or 4** — so
options **8** and **6** are impossible on sight ✗ They are values of 2ⁿ, not remainders.
That leaves 4 and 2, and the cycle position settles it: exponent ≡ 1 (mod 4) gives 2, while
≡ 2 would give 4.
∴ 2.

Expand the determinant to get a quadratic in x, then solve it.
**Step 1 — expand along the first row.** With
| x   2  −1 |
| 2   5   x |
| −1  2   x |
the expansion is
x[(5)(x) − (x)(2)] − 2[(2)(x) − (x)(−1)] + (−1)[(2)(2) − (5)(−1)]
**Step 2 — evaluate each 2 × 2 minor.**
first: 5x − 2x = **3x**
second: 2x + x = **3x**
third: 4 + 5 = **9**
**Step 3 — assemble**, minding the alternating signs + − +:
x(3x) − 2(3x) − 1(9)
= **3x² − 6x − 9**
**Step 4 — set it to zero and solve.**
3x² − 6x − 9 = 0
x² − 2x − 3 = 0 (dividing by 3)
**(x − 3)(x + 1) = 0**
**x = 3** or **x = −1** ✓
**Check x = 3.** The determinant becomes
| 3  2  −1 ; 2  5  3 ; −1  2  3 |
= 3(15 − 6) − 2(6 + 3) − 1(4 + 5)
= 27 − 18 − 9 = **0** ✓
**Check x = −1.**
| −1  2  −1 ; 2  5  −1 ; −1  2  −1 |
Here the **first and third rows are identical**, so the determinant is **0** ✓
immediately — a pleasing structural reason for that root, and a reminder that a repeated
row always forces a zero determinant.
**Reading the options by their sum and product.** From x² − 2x − 3 = 0, the roots sum to
**2** and multiply to **−3**. Testing:
**3, −1:** sum 2 ✓, product −3 ✓
**−3, 1:** sum −2 ✗
**3, 1:** sum 4 ✗
**−3, −1:** sum −4 ✗
Only one pair matches, and checking the sum alone is enough.
**Why expanding along the first row is convenient here.** The entry −1 in the top-right
keeps the third minor simple, and the two 3x terms that emerge combine cleanly. Expanding
along another row or column gives the same quadratic with more arithmetic.
∴ 3, −1.

The two diagonals of a square **bisect each other at right angles** and have **equal
length**, which locates the other two vertices at once.
**Step 1 — find the centre.** It is the midpoint of the given diagonal, from (0, −1) to
(0, 3):
centre = ((0 + 0)/2, (−1 + 3)/2) = **(0, 1)**
**Step 2 — find the length of the given diagonal.**
from (0, −1) to (0, 3) is **4** units, running **vertically** along the y-axis.
**Step 3 — describe the other diagonal.** It must
pass through the centre **(0, 1)** ✓
be **perpendicular** to the first, hence **horizontal**
have the same length, **4**, so it extends **2** units each side of the centre
**Step 4 — write the other two vertices.**
(0 + 2, 1) = **(2, 1)** and (0 − 2, 1) = **(−2, 1)** ✓
**Check all four sides are equal.** The vertices in order are (0, −1), (2, 1), (0, 3),
(−2, 1):
from (0,−1) to (2,1): √(4 + 4) = **2√2**
from (2,1) to (0,3): √(4 + 4) = **2√2**
from (0,3) to (−2,1): √(4 + 4) = **2√2**
from (−2,1) to (0,−1): √(4 + 4) = **2√2** ✓ all equal.
**Check a corner is a right angle.** At (2, 1), the two sides point along (−2, −2) and
(−2, 2), whose dot product is 4 − 4 = **0** ✓
**Check the diagonals.** Both are of length 4 ✓ and one is vertical while the other is
horizontal, so they are perpendicular ✓ Their midpoints are both (0, 1) ✓
**Reading the distractors.**
**(0, 1), (0, −3)** ✗ — these lie on the **same** line as the given pair, so no square is
formed.
**(3, −1), (0, 0)** ✗ — their midpoint is (1·5, −0·5), not the centre (0, 1).
**(2, 2), (1, 1)** ✗ — midpoint (1·5, 1·5), again not the centre.
The **midpoint test** is the quickest filter: the other two vertices must average to
**(0, 1)**, and only one option does ✓
∴ (2, 1), (−2, 1).

The quadratic part is a **perfect square**, so the whole equation is a quadratic in the
single quantity (x + y) — which is what makes the two lines parallel.
**Step 1 — recognise the perfect square.**
x² + 2xy + y² = **(x + y)²**
so the equation becomes
(x + y)² − 8a(x + y) − 9a² = 0
(since −8ax − 8ay = −8a(x + y).)
**Step 2 — substitute u = x + y.**
u² − 8au − 9a² = 0
**Step 3 — factorise**, looking for two numbers multiplying to −9a² and adding to −8a,
namely −9a and +a:
**(u − 9a)(u + a) = 0**
**u = 9a** or **u = −a**
**Step 4 — write the two lines.**
**x + y = 9a** and **x + y = −a**
They have the same left-hand side, so they are indeed **parallel** ✓ as the question
states.
**Step 5 — find the distance between them.** For ax + by + c₁ = 0 and ax + by + c₂ = 0,
distance = |c₁ − c₂|/√(a² + b²)
Here the lines are x + y − 9a = 0 and x + y + a = 0, so
distance = |−9a − a|/√(1² + 1²)
= 10|a|/√2
= **5√2 a** ✓
(rationalising 10/√2 = 10√2/2 = 5√2.)
**Check with a = 1.** The lines are x + y = 9 and x + y = −1. Taking the point (9, 0) on
the first, its distance to x + y + 1 = 0 is |9 + 0 + 1|/√2 = 10/√2 = **7·071**, and
5√2 = **7·071** ✓
**Why the two lines are 10a apart in constant but only 10a/√2 in distance.** The constants
differ by 10a, but the line x + y = c is tilted at 45°, so the perpendicular separation is
shortened by the factor √(1² + 1²) = √2 ✓

Using 1 + ω = −ω² (from the identity):
= −ω² − ω² = **−2ω²**
**Step 3 — simplify the second bracket.**
1 − x + x² = 1 − ω + ω²
Using 1 + ω² = −ω:
= −ω − ω = **−2ω**
**Step 4 — raise each to the sixth power.**
(−2ω²)⁶ = (−2)⁶ ω¹² = 64 ω¹²
(−2ω)⁶ = (−2)⁶ ω⁶ = 64 ω⁶
**Step 5 — reduce the powers of ω** using ω³ = 1:
ω¹² = (ω³)⁴ = **1**
ω⁶ = (ω³)² = **1**
**Step 6 — subtract.**
64(1) − 64(1) = **0** ✓

It exists uniquely **unless the three centres are collinear** — in which case the radical
axes are parallel and never meet.

**Step 2 — find the line through C₁ and C₂.**
gradient = (3 − 2)/(3 − 1) = **1/2**
through (1, 2): y − 2 = ½(x − 1), that is
**x − 2y + 3 = 0**
**Step 3 — ask when C₃ lies on that line.** Substituting (−k, −1):
(−k) − 2(−1) + 3 = −k + 2 + 3 = **5 − k**
This vanishes when
**k = 5**

parallel, and **no radical centre exists**. So the value k **cannot** take is **5** ✓
**Checking the other options are all fine.**
k = 1: C₃ = (−1, −1), and −1 + 2 + 3 = **4 ≠ 0** ✓ not collinear
k = 2: C₃ = (−2, −1), and −2 + 2 + 3 = **3 ≠ 0** ✓
k = 4: C₃ = (−4, −1), and −4 + 2 + 3 = **1 ≠ 0** ✓
Only k = 5 gives 0 ✗
**Why collinear centres kill the radical centre.** The radical axis of two circles is
always **perpendicular to the line joining their centres**. If all three centres lie on
one line, all three radical axes are perpendicular to that same line — hence **parallel**
to one another — and three parallel lines have no common point ✓
**A direct check at k = 5.** The third circle is x² + y² + 10x + 2y + 1 = 0.
radical axis of circles 1 and 2: subtracting, −4x − 2y + 1 = 0
radical axis of circles 2 and 3: subtracting, −12x − 6y + 2 = 0, that is −6x − 3y + 1 = 0
Their gradients are −2 and −2 — **equal**, so the lines are parallel and never meet ✓
confirming that no radical centre exists.
∴ 5.

and (−2, −1) are **not** collinear, so the radical centre exists perfectly well; the
value that must be excluded is 5, and the key has been corrected to the fourth option.

The two complex roots are (3 ± i√3)/2, which sum to **3**, and −3 + 3 = **0** ✓
The product of the roots is −9 (that is −constant for a monic cubic): the complex pair
multiply to 3, and 3 × (−3) = **−9** ✓

x = 6: 216 − 36 + 9 = **189** ✗
x = −6: −216 + 36 + 9 = **−171** ✗
x = −9: −729 + 54 + 9 = **−666** ✗
Only −3 gives zero, and substituting each candidate is the fastest route of all — four
short arithmetic checks.
**Why a cubic always has at least one real root.** As x → +∞ the cubic tends to +∞ and as
x → −∞ it tends to −∞, so by the intermediate value theorem it crosses zero somewhere.
Here it crosses exactly once, the other two roots being a complex conjugate pair ✓
∴ −3.

Powers of **5** are the easiest of all unit digits to track, because the pattern never
changes.
**Step 1 — look at the first few powers.**
5¹ = **5**
5² = 2**5**
5³ = 12**5**
5⁴ = 62**5**
Every one ends in **5**.
**Step 2 — see why it must continue.** If a number ends in 5, multiplying it by 5 gives a
number ending in 5 × 5 = 2**5** — again a final digit of 5. So the property is passed on
at every step, and by induction **every** positive power of 5 ends in 5 ✓
**Step 3 — apply it.** 5⁸³⁴ therefore has unit digit **5** ✓
**Why no cycle length is needed.** For most bases the unit digit repeats with a cycle —
powers of 2 cycle through 2, 4, 8, 6 with period 4, and powers of 3 through 3, 9, 7, 1 —
so the exponent must be reduced modulo the cycle length. For 5 the cycle has length
**1**: the digit is 5 no matter what the exponent is, so the enormous 834 is pure
decoration ✓
**The companion cases.** The same thing happens with **6**: 6, 36, 216, 1296, … all end
in 6. And **0**, **1** and **5** are likewise fixed. These four digits are the
**idempotent** ones modulo 10, satisfying d² ≡ d (mod 10):
0² = 0, 1² = 1, 5² = 25 ≡ 5, 6² = 36 ≡ 6 ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **0** would require a factor of 2 alongside the 5; 5⁸³⁴ is
odd, so it cannot end in 0 ✗ **1** and **3** are unit digits of powers of 3 and 7, not of
5 ✗ In fact the simplest observation settles it at once: 5⁸³⁴ is divisible by 5 and is
**odd**, and the only odd digit divisible by 5 is **5** ✓
∴ 5.

The notation (a, b) here means the **greatest common divisor**, and the equation
ax + by = 1 forces several of these to be 1 — but not all.
**The key principle.** If d divides **both** of two numbers, and the equation expresses 1
as a combination in which **both** appear with integer coefficients, then d divides 1, so
d = 1.
**Testing (a, b) = 1.** Let d divide a and b. Then d divides ax and by, hence their sum
**1**. So d = 1 ✓ **TRUE** — this is Bézout's theorem, and it is the statement the
equation is best known for.
**Testing (x, y) = 1.** Let d divide x and y. Then d divides ax and by, hence **1**. So
d = 1 ✓ **TRUE**
**Testing (a, y) = 1.** Let d divide a and y. Then d divides ax and by, hence **1** ✓
**TRUE**
**Testing (b, y) = 1.** Let d divide b and y. Then d divides by — but **not** necessarily
ax, since d has no stated relationship with a or x. The argument breaks down ✗
**The counter-example.** Take
a = 1, x = 5, b = 2, y = −2
then ax + by = 5 − 4 = **1** ✓ the condition holds, yet
(b, y) = (2, −2) = **2 ≠ 1** ✗
So the fourth statement is the one that is **not** true ✓
**Why the pattern is what it is.** Each product in ax + by pairs one letter from {a, b}
with one from {x, y} — a with x, and b with y. A common divisor of two numbers forces
them both into the same product only when the two numbers are taken from **different**
products:
(a, b): a is in the first, b in the second ✓ works
(x, y): x is in the first, y in the second ✓ works
(a, y): a is in the first, y in the second ✓ works
**(b, y): both are in the second product** ✗ fails
So the failing pair is the one whose members **multiply together** in the equation — here
b and y, since by is a single term.
**A second counter-example, for confidence.** a = 3, x = 3, b = 4, y = −2: 9 − 8 = **1** ✓
and (b, y) = (4, −2) = **2 ≠ 1** ✗
∴ (b, y) = 1 is the statement that is not true.

**Step 1 — the unit digit of 2009!** The factorial 2009! = 1 × 2 × 3 × ⋯ × 2009 contains

**0**

so the cycle is **3, 9, 7, 1** with length **4**.
**Step 3 — reduce the exponent modulo 4.**
7886 = 4 × 1971 + **2**

remainder would be 0 and the digit would be the **last** in the cycle, 3⁴ → **1**, not the

Row operations reduce the determinant to a single simple condition on a, b and c.
**Step 1 — subtract adjacent rows.** With
| x+1  x+2  x+a |
| x+2  x+3  x+b |
| x+3  x+4  x+c |
replace R₂ by R₂ − R₁ and R₃ by R₃ − R₂ (operations that leave the determinant
unchanged):
R₂ − R₁ = **(1, 1, b − a)**
R₃ − R₂ = **(1, 1, c − b)**
giving
| x+1  x+2  x+a |
|  1    1   b−a |
|  1    1   c−b |
The x has vanished from two of the three rows — which is why the answer does not depend
on x.
**Step 2 — subtract again.** Replacing R₃ by R₃ − R₂:
R₃ − R₂ = **(0, 0, (c − b) − (b − a))**
so the last row is (0, 0, c − 2b + a).
**Step 3 — expand.** With two zeros in the last row, the determinant is simply
(c − 2b + a) × | x+1  x+2 ; 1  1 |
= (c − 2b + a) × [(x + 1) − (x + 2)]
= (c − 2b + a) × (**−1**)
**Step 4 — set it to zero.**
−(a − 2b + c) = 0
**a + c = 2b**
**Step 5 — interpret.** a + c = 2b says b is the **arithmetic mean** of a and c, which is
exactly the condition for
**a, b, c to be in A.P.** ✓
**Check with an A.P.** Take a = 1, b = 2, c = 3 and x = 0:
| 1  2  1 ; 2  3  2 ; 3  4  3 |
The first and third **columns are identical**, so the determinant is **0** ✓
**Check with a non-A.P.** Take a = 1, b = 2, c = 4 and x = 0:
| 1  2  1 ; 2  3  2 ; 3  4  4 |
= 1(12 − 8) − 2(8 − 6) + 1(8 − 9) = 4 − 4 − 1 = **−1 ≠ 0** ✓ consistent, since 1, 2, 4 is
not an A.P.
**Why the first two columns do the work.** They differ by the constant vector (1, 1, 1)
in every row, so the only information in the determinant comes from how the **third**
column deviates from that same constant step — and a constant step is precisely an
arithmetic progression ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **G.P.** would need b² = ac, **H.P.** would need
2/b = 1/a + 1/c, and **equal** is the special case a = b = c. All three are **sufficient**
in the last case but none is the general condition, which is the A.P. relation a + c = 2b.
∴ in A.P.

The dot product reaches **−|ā||b̄|**, its smallest possible value, only when the cosine
is at its minimum.
**Step 1 — write the definition.**
ā · b̄ = |ā| |b̄| cos θ
**Step 2 — compare with what is given.**
|ā| |b̄| cos θ = −|ā| |b̄|
**Step 3 — divide by |ā||b̄|**, which is non-zero (otherwise no angle would be defined):
**cos θ = −1**
**Step 4 — solve.** The only angle in [0°, 180°] with cosine −1 is
**θ = 180°** ✓
**What this means geometrically.** The two vectors point in **exactly opposite**
directions — they are **antiparallel**. One is a negative multiple of the other:
b̄ = −λā for some λ > 0.
**Checking with an example.** Take ā = (1, 0, 0) and b̄ = (−3, 0, 0):
ā · b̄ = **−3**
|ā| |b̄| = 1 × 3 = **3**
so ā · b̄ = −|ā||b̄| ✓ and the vectors plainly point opposite ways, an angle of 180° ✓
**The full range of the dot product.** Since −1 ≤ cos θ ≤ 1,
**−|ā||b̄| ≤ ā · b̄ ≤ |ā||b̄|**
with the **maximum** |ā||b̄| at θ = 0° (parallel, same direction) and the **minimum**
−|ā||b̄| at θ = 180° (antiparallel). The question gives the extreme negative value, so the
angle must be the extreme 180° ✓
**Checking the other options.**
**60°:** cos = 0·5, giving ā·b̄ = +0·5|ā||b̄| ✗ positive
**45°:** cos = 0·707 ✗ positive
**90°:** cos = 0, giving ā·b̄ = **0** ✗ — this is the condition for **perpendicular**
vectors, and it is the commonest wrong answer, since a dot-product condition is often
associated with perpendicularity.
The **sign** is what distinguishes them: ā·b̄ = 0 means perpendicular, while
ā·b̄ = −|ā||b̄| means directly opposed ✓
**The companion condition with the cross product.** |ā × b̄| = |ā||b̄| would mean
sin θ = 1, that is θ = **90°**. So the dot product detects parallelism and the cross
product detects perpendicularity — each extreme corresponding to the other's zero.
∴ 180°.
